Ramah
RAY-muh
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Ramah (H7414), "height, high place" (from rum, "to be high"). Several towns bear the name; chiefly Ramah of Benjamin / Ephraim, the home of Samuel, and Ramah associated with Rachel's weeping.

Biblical Definition

Ramah ("height") was the name of several towns in Israel, the most significant being the Ramah that was the home, judgment-seat, and burial place of the prophet Samuel, and the Ramah associated in prophecy with Rachel weeping for her children. Samuel's Ramah (Ramathaim-zophim) was the town of his father Elkanah and his mother Hannah (1 Sam 1:1, 19); it was Samuel's home throughout his life, the seat from which he judged Israel on his yearly circuit (1 Sam 7:17), the place to which the elders of Israel came to demand a king (1 Sam 8:4), and the place of his death and burial, where all Israel mourned him (1 Sam 25:1). It was at Ramah, in the company of the prophets, that David fled to Samuel from Saul, and where the Spirit of God came mightily even upon Saul's messengers and upon Saul himself (1 Sam 19:18-24). The other great association of Ramah is prophetic and sorrowful: Jeremiah, foreseeing the exile, wrote, "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not" (Jer 31:15) — Ramah being near where the captives were gathered for deportation, and near Rachel's traditional burial place. The Gospel of Matthew applies this very verse to the slaughter of the innocents at Bethlehem by Herod, when the children were killed in the attempt to destroy the infant Christ (Matt 2:17-18). Ramah thus carries a double weight: the place of Samuel the great prophet and intercessor, and the place of the deepest maternal grief, taken up by the Spirit to describe both the sorrow of the exile and the sorrow of Bethlehem — grief that, in Jeremiah's own context, is immediately followed by the promise of the new covenant and the return (Jer 31:16-17, 31-34).

Webster 1828 Definition

A town ("height") chiefly known as the home, judgment-seat, and burial place of Samuel (1 Sam 1; 7:17; 25:1), and as the place of Rachel weeping for her children (Jer 31:15), a verse Matthew applies to Herod's slaughter of the innocents at Bethlehem (Matt 2:17-18).

RAMAH, proper noun. Hebrew Ramah (H7414), "height, high place"; the name of several towns.

Chiefly the home of Samuel (Ramathaim-zophim), town of Elkanah and Hannah (1 Sam 1:1, 19).

Samuel's lifelong home and judgment-seat (1 Sam 7:17); where Israel demanded a king (1 Sam 8:4); his death and burial place (1 Sam 25:1).

Where David fled to Samuel and the Spirit came on Saul's messengers and on Saul (1 Sam 19:18-24).

"A voice was heard in Ramah... Rahel weeping for her children" (Jer 31:15); applied by Matthew to Herod's slaughter at Bethlehem (Matt 2:17-18).

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 7:17 — "And his return was to Ramah; for there was his house; and there he judged Israel; and there he built an altar unto the LORD."

1 Samuel 25:1 — "And Samuel died; and all the Israelites were gathered together, and lamented him, and buried him in his house at Ramah."

Jeremiah 31:15-16 — "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted... Thus saith the LORD; Refrain thy voice from weeping... and they shall come again from the land of the enemy."

Matthew 2:17-18 — "Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not."

Modern Corruption

Ramah is corrupted when its several locations are confused without care, when the Jeremiah 31:15 lament is severed from its context of new-covenant hope, or when Matthew's application of it to the slaughter of the innocents is misread as a strained proof-text rather than a Spirit-given connection.

expand to see more

Lament-severed-from-hope. Jeremiah 31:15, "a voice was heard in Ramah... Rachel weeping for her children," is one of the most sorrowful verses in Scripture, and it is sometimes quoted as a bare expression of grief. In Jeremiah its setting is crucial: the very next verses turn from weeping to hope — "Refrain thy voice from weeping... thy children shall come again" (Jer 31:16-17) — and the same chapter contains the great promise of the new covenant (Jer 31:31-34). The weeping of Ramah is real, but it is bounded by the promise of return and of the new covenant in Christ. The Spirit who recorded the lament recorded also the comfort.

Matthew's-application misread. Matthew applies Jeremiah's "voice in Ramah" to the weeping at Bethlehem when Herod slaughtered the infants in his attempt to kill the child Christ (Matt 2:17-18). Critics sometimes treat this as a strained or arbitrary proof-text. The connection is rich and deliberate: as Israel wept when the children were carried into exile, so the mothers of Bethlehem wept when the children were slain — and in both cases the weeping is taken up into the larger purpose of God, who brings His people back from exile and who preserves His Son through the slaughter to accomplish the redemption that turns weeping into joy. Matthew, writing by the same Spirit who inspired Jeremiah, draws the line the Spirit intended.

Hebrew Roots

A town ("height") chiefly the home, judgment-seat, and burial place of Samuel (1 Sam 1; 7:17; 25:1), and the place of Rachel weeping for her children (Jer 31:15), applied by Matthew to Herod's slaughter at Bethlehem (Matt 2:17-18).
